title: Call and response
hook: the preacher calls, the people answer: worship as conversation

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying for healing: bold asking, and open hands about the answer. Your line was by his stripes. Who did you show up for? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

The preacher is deep into the sermon now, and she isn't talking alone. She says a line, and from the third pew someone answers, "Well!" She says the next one, and from the back, "Preach!" An organ chord fills the gap. She slows down, leans on the pulpit, and asks the room, "Can I get a witness?" The room answers, "Amen!" In the Black church tradition, none of that is an interruption. It's how the sermon gets preached. The preacher calls, the people answer, and worship turns into a conversation. Today: call and response.

The shape is in the Bible too. In Nehemiah, the people gather in the street before the Water Gate in Jerusalem to hear Ezra read the law. When he opens the book, he blesses God. The text says: "And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God. And all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands." A call, and an answer. Amen is the people's word: yes, so be it, this is true. Paul takes the same thing for granted when he writes to Corinth. He asks how a listener who can't follow the prayer could "say Amen at thy giving of thanks." In his churches, people answered. Now the word in today's line: witness. A witness, in a courtroom or in the Bible, is someone who tells what they saw. Before he leaves, Jesus tells his followers in Acts, "ye shall be witnesses unto me." So when a preacher asks, "Can I get a witness?" the question underneath is: has anybody else seen this? Is this true in your life too? The amen that comes back isn't applause for the preacher. It's testimony that the word holds. And the conversation runs both ways. A preacher in this tradition listens to the room. When the answers come quick, the sermon builds. When the room goes quiet, the preacher may circle back and say it again, slower, until it lands. The people help carry the sermon. Here's what that means on an ordinary weekday. In call and response, nobody is just the audience. Every voice in the room has a job, even if the job is one word.
screen: `SAY AMEN AT THY GIVING OF THANKS.`
`A WITNESS SAYS: I SAW IT TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say amen out loud when you agree. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a line of scripture you know, or a sentence someone once said to you that turned out to be true. Hold it a moment. If you find you agree with it, answer it out loud: amen. It can be quiet. Then find another true thing, a kindness you received or a lesson you learned the hard way, and answer that one too. Notice what changes when you answer instead of only listening. The bell holds the time.
Call and response. The preacher calls, the people answer, and the sermon is preached by the whole room.
Your line: can I get a witness? Today, when someone says something true, at work, at home, in a group chat, answer it. Say so out loud. Be their witness. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: In Black church worship, congregations answer the preacher during the sermon with words like amen, well and preach, and the preacher listens and responds to them, so the sermon is shaped by the whole room.

what a scholar hears: the answering amen runs through scripture, from Ezra's reading in Nehemiah to Paul, who assumes listeners will say Amen.

notes: Audit pass (2026-10-02): all KJV quotations checked word for word against the cited verses; attributions, framing and nearby days (1162–1181) checked for repetition. No change needed.
The hook's service is a composite scene (responses 'Well!', 'Preach!', an organ, 'Can I get a witness?'); confirm it is a fair and respectful picture of Black church preaching.
No historical-origin claim is made about call and response (e.g. West African roots) under the claims rule; a Keeper may want one added with a source.
Nehemiah 8:1 places the reading in 'the street that was before the water gate'; the script says 'a square in Jerusalem'. Confirm or change to 'an open place by the Water Gate'.
'Before he leaves' for Acts 1:8 refers to the ascension context (Acts 1:9); confirm.
Original: אָמֵן glossed 'so be it, truly' without an etymology; confirm.
